actions.name: Occurs in at least one protected area

documentation.range: This species was previously only known from only two localities, both in Idukki District in the Cardomom Hills in Kerala: Kattapana; and near Idukki town. It is now known to occur from the western slopes of Western Ghats continuously from north of Shencottah Gap to Wayanaad (S. Das pers. comm. October 2020). In Kerala, it is known from Kothamangalam in Ernakulam District, Erumely in Kottayam District (Dutta et al. 2004), Silent Valley National Park in  Palakkad District (Das 2006), Karuvarakundu in Malappuram District (Radhakrishnan et al. 2007), Pattikkad Range in Thrissur Forest Division, Poringalkuthu in Vazhachal, Thrissur District, Peechi-Vazhani Wildlife Sanctuary (Jobin et al. 2012), and Nadukani–Moolamattom–Kulamaav tribal settlement (Thomas and. Biju 2015). It is also present in Tamil Nadu State, in Sankaran Kudi in the Anamalai (Dutta et al. 2004) and Karian Shola in Anamalai Tiger Reserve (Raj et al. 2011). It is found in Periyar Tiger Reserve, Idukki Wildlife Sanctuary, Thattekad Wildlife Sanctuary, Vazhchal Reserve Forests, Ranni Forest Division, Konni Division, Mankulam Reserve Forests, Chimmony Wildlife Sanctuary, Peechi Wildlife Sanctuary, Nelliyampathy Reserve Forests, Nilambur Reserve Forests, Mannarkad Forest Division, Silent Valley National Park, Karimpuzha Wildlife Sanctuary, Idukki, Wagamon, Nilambur, Karuvarakkundu, Ambanad, Dhoni, Vazhazchal, Valparai, Malakkapara, and Parambikulam Tiger Reserve (S. Das pers. comm. October 2020). Tadpole records are known from Anappantham Forest (N. Modak, P.O. Nameer and S. Swami pers. comm. October 2020). It occurs between 30–1,400 m asl (Zachariah et al. 2012; S. Das pers. comm. October 2020). This is likely to be its full distribution (S. Das pers. comm. October 2020). Its extent of occurrence (EOO) is 19,480 km2.
documentation.population: It is considered to be common, but it is hard to find due to its fossorial behaviour (it surfaces for only a couple hours during a single day a year - S. Das pers. comm. October 2020). More than 1,000 breeding pairs have been observed from 2011 until now (S. Das pers. comm. October 2020). Due to ongoing decline in the extent and quality of its habitat, the population is inferred to be decreasing.
documentation.habitats: This species has been found in disturbed secondary forest contiguous with montane evergreen forest, in undisturbed forest as well (though apparently it does not survive in open, completely cleared habitats). For most of the year it is a fossorial species, living from 1.3–3.7m below ground (S. Das pers. comm. October 2020). It comes to the surface for between 2–4 hours (within a single day) a year to breed in stagnant pools which are connected to seasonal streams (S. Das pers. comm. October 2020). It is an explosive breeder, and eggs are laid in seasonal streams during the pre-monsoon rains, and hatch before the monsoon intensifies and the tadpoles disperse with the flowing stream (Zachariah et al. 2012, Thomas et al. 2019).
documentation.threats:
There is an ongoing loss of natural habitats due to anthropogenic disturbance over much of the Western Ghats. This is caused by the development of roads and road widening (India Red List Assessment Workshop October 2020), small-scale plantations (coffee, cardamom, ginger and other species), illegal encroachment and unsustainable harvesting of tree species. Granite quarrying for construction is a major threat throughout its range, and landslides which can occur throughout the species' range and will be a problem with one a year occurring since 2018 (India Red List Assessment Workshop October 2020). Human activities of road building and quarrying can cause these landslides (India Red List Assessment Workshop October 2020). An additional threat is dam construction - with extensive small check dams both outside and inside protected areas (Dutta et al. 2004, Aggarwal 2004), which will affect the streams used by this species for breeding and cause flooding (S. Das pers. comm. October 2020). Road mortalities are considered to be a major threat particularly in areas in Idukki e.g. one observation on a 2 km stretch included 36 dead breeding pairs of this species within Nelliyampathi Reserve Forest, along with noise from road traffic which may also interfere with their acoustic communication (S. Das pers. comm. October 2020). Furthermore, tourism affects its habitat through pollution (e.g. glass bottles) which is detrimental to eggs, tadpoles and adults through clogging oviposition sites and causing mortalities (S. Das pers. comm. October 2020).

As eggs hatch to tadpoles within seven days, climate is a potential future threat as any changes in rainfall could cause the drying of its breeding sites or excessive rainfall will result in the mortality of tadpoles and loss of egg clutches (S. Das pers. comm. October 2020).

This species has been swabbed for Batrachochytrium dendrobatidis (Bd) with mixed results, may be a potential threat for this species but further research is required (K. Krutha and S. Das pers. comm. October 2020). Due to its fossorial behaviour, it is difficult to access individuals for testing (S. Das pers. comm. October 2020. Observations of mouth abnormalities in Nasikabtarachus sahyadrensis have been recorded (Vasudevan 2010), which could be indicative of Batrachochytrium dendrobatidis (Bd) although the exact cause has not be confirmed and further study is required (K. Vasudevan pers. comm. December 2020).
documentation.measures:
Conservation Actions In-Place
This species occurs in many protected areas including Silent Valley National Park, Anamalai Tiger Reserve, Peechi-Vazhani Wildlife Sanctuary, Nadukani–Moolamattom–Kulamaav tribal settlement, Periyar Tiger Reserve, Idukki Wildlife Sanctuary, Thattekad Wildlife Sanctuary, Vazhchal Reserve Forests, Mankulam Reserve Forests, Chimmony Wildlife Sanctuary, Peechi Wildlife Sanctuary, Nelliyampathy Reserve Forests, Nilambur Reserve Forests, Karimpuzha Wildlife Sanctuary and Parambikulam Tiger Reserve, with % of the population occurring in these areas (S. Das pers. comm. October 2020). Awareness campaigns are ongoing among tribal and local people designed specifically to educate and provide them with basic amenities and employment opportunities.

Conservation Needed
Improved habitat protection is required.

Research Needed
The most important conservation measures proposed for this taxon are long-term monitoring. Additional surveys on specific local threats are also needed (Thomas and Biju 2015), including the effects of Bd and climate change, and its fossorial ecology (India Red List Assessment Workshop October 2020).
documentation.use_trade: This frog´s tadpoles are harvested for subsistence consumption by tribal and local communities. However, a five-year study on the impact of tadpole collection for human consumption by tribal or indigenous communities concluded it was impossible to confidently infer a relation between tadpole decline and harvesting because of the severe population fluctuations this taxon experiences due to stochastic factors (Thomas and Biju 2015). Harvesting as an activity is thought to be in decline, and is more associated with older members of local communities (S. Das pers. comm. October 2020). It is also used for medicinal properties to combat asthma (Kanagavel et al. 2020). Adults and larvae are consumed specifically by children and infants as medicine for skin-based ailments, cold, cough, throat infection, asthma, measles, chicken pox and stomach pain. They are consumed after cooking or after drying and/or powdered or vapours from burning the dried frog are inhaled. Fat tissue/mucous lining is applied on external wounds. Small-sized individuals, skin, limbs, or digit ends are used as amulets for children to reduce fear, when they are unable to sleep at night or who do not speak or walk well  (Kanagavel et al. 2020).
documentation.rationale: Listed as Near Threatened because its extent of occurrence (EOO) is 19,480 km<sup>2</sup> and there is continuing decline in the extent and quality of its habitat. However it is thought to occur in more than ten threat-defined locations and its population is probably not severely fragmented. It is therefore close to qualifying for Vulnerable under criterion B1.
documentation.taxonomic_notes: This species has been reported from several additional localities, although these likely refer to undescribed species (S.D. Biju pers. comm.)
